'My judgment fell short, but…': Chuck Edwards' ‘beyond inappropriate’ conduct sparks House rebuke
Republican Congressman Chuck Edwards has been censured by the U.S. House in an overwhelming 413–2 vote following a House Ethics Committee investigation into his conduct toward two female staffers.

The House of Representatives voted to censure outgoing Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-NC) after the House Ethics Committee investigated allegations that he sexually harassed young female staffers in his office.
In a 413-2 vote, the House imposed its strongest punishment short of expulsion.
Although Edwards denied the allegations, he ended his re-election campaign after the committee published its findings.
“Following the vote, Rep. Edwards stood in well of the House while Speaker Johnson read the censure resolution against him from the chair,” C-SPAN wrote.
Watch below:
U.S. House CENSURES Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-NC).
Following the vote, Rep. Edwards stood in well of the House while Speaker Johnson read the censure resolution against him from the chair. pic.twitter.com/kUqIdTaJvq
— CSPAN (@cspan) September 1, 2026
POLITICO has more:
It also comes as Congress is grappling with how to protect aides from members’ bad behavior amid a rash of harassment and assault allegations against lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.
ADVERTISEMENT
In Edwards’ case, the Ethics Committee found the lawmaker participated in “persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers” and made comments on the appearance of his aides, including on one staffer’s weight.
According to the report, Edwards gave the female aides purses, guns, shoes and flowers. Edwards skipped House votes one night to decorate a Christmas tree with a staffer and went drinking and gambling with her. The lawmaker recited a poem at her departure celebration and cried during it, making the staff uncomfortable, the committee said.
“Neither individual felt free to reject Rep. Edwards’ attention without fear of professional consequences,” said Rep. Mark Desaulnier of California, the top Democrat on the Ethics panel, during floor debate on the censure measure.
Edwards defended himself on the House Floor amid the vote.
“Generosity is not sexual harassment. Caring deeply about the people with whom you’ve worked for years is not sexual harassment,” he said.
Watch below:
.@RepChuckEdwards (R-NC) defends himself during U.S. House debate to censure him for misconduct: "Generosity is not sexual harassment. Caring deeply about the people with whom you've worked for years is not sexual harassment." pic.twitter.com/k6DmlqcDoO
— CSPAN (@cspan) September 1, 2026
NPR shared further:
Speaking from the House floor ahead of the censure vote, Edwards pleaded with his colleagues to “judge me on the facts, not on the inference, insinuation or headlines.”
He apologized to the two staffers at the center of the investigation, saying, “I recognize now that my understanding of those relationships may not have always matched yours.” He insisted, however, that “regret is not an admission of sexual harassment.”
The House Ethics panel recommended the censure as part of an Aug. 3 report on their investigation — a report that determined he “engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.”
The committee found he created a hostile work environment, citing “substantial evidence” he “violated the spirit of the House’s prohibition on sexual harassment and unwanted advances.”

This story was originally reported by Mel Leonor Barclay of The 19th. Meet Mel and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
House lawmakers formally censured Republican Rep. Chuck Edwards of North Carolina over findings that he behaved inappropriately toward two women staffers, showering them with gifts and attention, including reciting poetry for one and giving each a personalized handgun.
The resolution was backed by members of both parties with overwhelming support. The vote marked a rare moment where a member of the party in power faced disciplinary action in the form of censure, and where that action stemmed from inappropriate conduct toward women. A censure doesn’t carry any practical consequences but is rare enough to show deep disapproval of the conduct among lawmakers. How and if Edwards will be punished would require a separate vote.
Edwards abandoned his reelection campaign last month amid growing attention on the accusations and details of his behavior.
The bipartisan House Ethics Committee found in August that Edwards had failed to “adhere to the spirit of rules prohibiting sexual harassment of and unwanted advances to House staffers.” The committee found that Edwards had directed “excessive attention” toward the young women, including writing and tearfully reciting a poem for one staffer, sending handwritten notes and gifts, and inviting or pressuring the staffers on social outings.
According to the committee, Edwards showered both staffers with gifts, including “jewelry totaling over $1,000, designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, a robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners.” The guns had personalized engravings, according to the committee’s report.
Edwards vehemently denies that he violated House rules. In comments on the House floor Tuesday ahead of the censure vote, Edwards apologized to the two staff members, but disputed that he had sexually harassed them.
“I’m sorry that my actions, my judgment or the way that I expressed a friendship ever put either of you in an uncomfortable position,” Edwards said. “Regret is not an admission of sexual harassment. I can acknowledge poor judgment, regret about the discomfort some of my actions may have caused, and apologize to those who were hurt by this episode while still disputing a conclusion that the evidence simply does not support.”
The censure vote came amid an ongoing campaign by women lawmakers from both parties urging Congress to clamp down on sexual misconduct among lawmakers and staffers. The censure vote taking place on the House’s first full day back after the summer recess and just weeks before Election Day puts a strong spotlight on sexual harassment and workplace misconduct toward women.
Edwards is one of four congressmen this year who will leave their seats after facing accusations of misconduct against women.
Republican voters in Florida rejected Rep. Cory Mills’ reelection bid last month after he faced allegations that he assaulted a woman and threatened to publicize nude videos of a former girlfriend, among other possible misconduct. He has denied wrongdoing.
Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas resigned in April after facing accusations of sexual coercion involving a staffer; Democratic Rep. Eric Swalwell of California resigned on the same day after facing accusations of sexual assault. Both men were facing expulsion when they resigned. Gonzales admitted to the affair and called it a “lapse in judgment.” Swalwell has said the allegations against him are false.
Heading into November, Republicans will be defending a fifth congressman accused of misconduct against women: Rep. Max Miller, who represents Ohio’s 7th Congressional District, is facing serious allegations of domestic violence against his ex-wife and young daughter. Miller continues to vehemently deny the accusations of abuse, but the scandal has given Democrats an opening in a previously safe Republican district.
Had he raped them, however, he’d be considered a good candidate to lead the newly reorganized Pentagon — the Mentagone — as soon as Pisco Packin’ Pete is shown the cargo bay door without a parachute. OTOH had the women been underage and he raped and even threatened to kill them, the Guardians Of Pedophiles would be slobbering and falling all over themselves to determine whether he should run as President or Vice President in '28.
Not impressed. The censure won’t mean all that much when he’s already withdrawn from his election campaign.

On Sept. 1, the US House of Representatives voted 413-2 to censure US Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-NC11, following a recent report from the House Ethics Committee finding him to be in violation of the House Official Code of Conduct prohibiting sexual harassment.
The total number of votes to censure Edwards was 207 Republicans and 205 Democrats. Edwards himself and US Rep. Ralph Norman, R-SC5, were the two nay votes; 17 abstained from the vote.
I respect the House vote. I do not accept the conclusion that it produced.
The Committee found no sexual activity, no proposition, no quid pro quo, and no violation of federal sexual-harassment law. It then crossed the gap between those facts and a finding of sexual harassment…
— Congressman Chuck Edwards (@RepChuckEdwards) September 1, 2026
“Sexual harassment is serious. It should be treated seriously,” wrote Edwards in an X post. “But that seriousness is precisely why we should not redefine ordinary acts of friendship, generosity, encouragement, or compassion as something they were not. I have apologized for where my judgment fell short. But I will not confess to conduct I did not commit simply to make this moment easier. The House has spoken. So have I. I will leave this chapter with my head held high and finish the job Western North Carolina sent me here to do.”
On Aug. 25, Edwards sent a letter to his colleagues defending himself against the committee’s report and making a final appeal. Edwards asserts in the letter that the committee took an “extraordinary analytical leap” from the evidence to the conclusion. Edwards continues to assert that there is a great distance between the evidence presented and the conclusion the committee came to and that the committee went well beyond the scope of the evidence to conclude sexual harassment.
The allegations against Edwards involved two young female staffers who had both worked in Edwards congressional office. During his remarks on the House Floor, Edwards apologized to his family and staffers and clarified that his apology did not constitute an admission of guilt.
“I’m sorry that my actions, my judgment or the way that I expressed a friendship ever put either of you in an uncomfortable position,” said Edwards. “Regret is not an admission of sexual harassment.”
“I can acknowledge poor judgment, regret the discomfort that some of my actions may have caused and apologize to those who were hurt by this episode while still disputing a conclusion that the evidence just simply does not support,” continued Edwards.
On Aug. 4 at 3:32am, Edwards announced in an X post that he would not be seeking re-election in the upcoming November midterms.
“Given the Ethics Committee’s recommendation to censure and the current sensitivity to sexual issues in Congress, the vote to censure him was inevitable,” Andy Jasckson, director of the Civitas Center for Public Integrity at the John Locke Foundation, told the Carolina Journal. “Other than posturing back in the 11th District to make some political hay out of Edward’s conduct, this will be the end of it. While the committee did not accuse Edwards of ever seeking sex from the two young staffers, they found that the gifts and travel perks he lavished on them ‘violated the spirit’ of House rules and created a hostile work environment.”
In his place, state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom, R-Henderson, has been tapped by Republicans as the GOP nominee to run in the 11th Congressional District against Democrat Jamie Ager.
On Aug. 17, President Donald Trump endorsed Balkcom in a Truth Social post.

(The Center Square) – Late to the race and only because Rep. Chuck Edwards was ensnared in an ethics complaint, Republican congressional candidate Jennifer Balkcom is gaining endorsements – many expected from her party – in North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District.
Balkcom, state House of Representatives member from Henderson County, is challenged by Fairview’s Jamie Ager on the Democrats’ ticket and Greensboro’s Travis Groo on the Libertarian ticket.
The 11th is in the mountains, from Avery to McDowell and Polk counties north-south extending to the southwestern tip of the state. It's the heart of cleanup from Hurricane Helene’s remnants coming through in September 2024.
The district was carried by Trump three times, including by 10% in 2024. Seven times by three men, the district has gone to Republicans since the 2010 win by Democratic Rep. Heath Shuler.
The seat has grown to be pivotal to majority power in the U.S. House, in part because Ager was building more strength fiscally before Edwards left the race, and in part because Edwards did leave the race. Republicans' 220-215 edge won in November 2024 is today 218-212 with one independent formerly Republican caucusing with his former party, and four vacancies.
Balkcom and Ager dueled last week in a candidate forum on agriculture. She also last week picked up the endorsement of sixth-term Republican state Agriculture Commissioner Steve Troxler.
Balkcom grew up on a farm and has professional experience as a small business owner for mortgage loans, and serving on boards for education, healthcare and infrastructure planning. Ager works about 250 acres of farmland, some owned and some leased, raising beef cattle, pigs, chickens and turkeys.
“As a Henderson County farm girl, she understands firsthand the vital role agriculture plays in our towns, our economy, and our way of life,” Troxler said. “Jennifer spent her time in the General Assembly standing up for our farmers, families, small businesses, and rural communities. She will take her mountain values to D.C., work with President Trump to rebuild western North Carolina, and make sure our government works for the people – not against them.”
Others voicing approval are also in the Republican Party and thus expected. They are led by second-term Republican President Donald Trump; House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.; House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La.; Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn.; and Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., the chairwoman of the House Majority Conference.
A statement from Johnson representing the party leaders said in part, “As a state representative and eighth generation western North Carolinian, Jennifer will bring her experience and values to Congress to protect girls’ sports, support our farmers, cut burdensome regulations, and defend the principles that have made America the greatest nation on Earth.”
Balkcom worked this session on Jones Street with Republican Reps. Donnie Loftis of Gaston County, Brian Biggs of Randolph County and Larry Potts of Davidson County on the Parents’ Medical Bill of Rights. Known also as House Bill 519, it stalled May 7, 2025, in the Senate’s rule committee following 68-41 passage – including four Democrats, though one is now independent – in the House of Representatives.
The proposal says consent from parents or guardians for minors getting medical treatment will be required before physicians can act. The legislation makes exceptions for emergency treatments needed to save a child’s life or for treatment of a child whose identity is unknown.
It also exempts treatment for suspected abuse that doctors are other health care professionals already required under North Carolina to be reported to authorities.
“One of my favorite bills,” Balkcom says. “All parents want to know about their child’s health, period.”
Ager’s endorsements include former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg; Reproductive Freedom for All; the 314 Action Fund; Democrats Work for America; and Big Tent Democrats. Three opponents in the March 3 primary cried foul when the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee in February put its support behind Ager.
In the statement of endorsement from the ever-mercurial Trump, he praised her civic engagement and service to community while taking a shot at Ager.
He said, in part, Ager “is a radical left Democrat who is opposed to no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, and no tax on Social Security.” He said if Ager and Democrats “ever got in, all of these things will be terminated.
“Jennifer will fight tirelessly to grow our economy, champion our amazing farmers and ranchers, cut taxes and regulations, unleash American energy dominance, promote ‘Made in the USA,’ strengthen our brave military/veterans, keep our border secure, safeguard our elections, and protect our always under siege Second Amendment.”
